evidences.title: African migrant workers find slim pickings in southern Spain | Spain | The Guardian
evidences.content:
In the huge, air-conditioned shed the conveyor belts carrying a stream of punnets have slowed. The workforce has shrunk, too, at Bionest, the biggest organic strawberry grower in Andaluca. In the fields and in the hectares of plastic-covered hothouses there is little sign of work being done. By early June the season is nearly over, particularly as this year the weather was poor, spoiling the yield of strawberries, raspberries and blueberries on which the local economy depends.

In the streets of Almonte, near Huelva, south-east Spain, groups of women are waiting for the coach to go back to Bucharest or Tangiers. Most pickers here are Romanian or Moroccan women, coming back each year in early spring. Three or four months later, depending on their contract, they leave with enough money to see them through to the following season.

Moussa Diarra, 22, from Mali, has no intention of moving. He landed in Spain two years ago in an open boat and has no return ticket. He is one of the "ghosts" who have haunted nearby woods in recent years. Just outside Palos de la Frontera, some 1,500 to 2,000 Africans have built shacks with scrap wood and plastic sheets from the hothouses. This is the end of the line for these men who once thought they could make good picking fruit.

None of them found work in the fields this season. "They don't like blacks; all they want is women," says Draman Bari, 41, from Senegal. He has been stuck here for four years. The growers now refuse to employ anyone without a permit. About 15 years ago they started switching to a workforce from selected "countries of origin" with temporary permits.

"The crisis has made [getting] papers pointless. It's got to stop. Even at home it's better than Spain at present," explains Abou Sidib, 45, a Malian who obtained a permit several years ago. "We are on the spot. Why don't they give us contracts instead of importing workers?" Diarra asks.

But even now a little work can make all the difference. "Last year I worked for two weeks planting strawberries. That paid for one year's schooling for my three little brothers in Burkina [Faso]," says Sawadogo Seidou, 27.

Two years ago, in an attempt to halt immigration, Spain reduced the number of temporary contracts allocated to the countries of origin, from 183,600 in 2007 to less than 20,000 last year. Fruit pickers in the Huelva area are the largest contingent and even their numbers have dropped, from 16,500 in 2009 to 4,500 this year.

Spain (population 47 million) no longer attracts so many immigrants. Unemployment, which affects more than 20% of the active population, has hit immigrants hardest, with almost a third jobless. Some 100,000 Latin Americans went home in 2009, mainly to Ecuador (26,500), Bolivia (20,000) and Argentina (11,700). Immigrants now number 5.7 million, accounting for 12% of the total, and the Spanish have started looking for work elsewhere. Last year more people left the country (102,000) than settled here from abroad (60,270).

In the Huelva area, hit by the downturn in the building industry, the population is keen to return to the fields. "This year, after talking to the regional authorities, we signed up local people too," says Juan Soltero, the manager at Bionest. But such contracts only represent a tiny proportion of the total.

Diego Canamero, general secretary of the Farm Workers union (SOC), says: "The reason they prefer to sign contracts with the countries of origin, when there are endless queues outside the job centres in Seville and Cdiz, is that those workers have fewer rights than us." When Soltero cites "the shortage of local labour" to justify his position, Canamero explodes: "It's just not true that a third of Andaluca's jobless are refusing work. The government is trying to cover up the scale of unemployment."

In Spain the minimum wage is $45.20 a day, but closer to $40 once rent, transport to the fields and other items have been deducted. If you work every day it is supposed to add up to more than $1,200 a month, but that does not allow for bad weather.

Most of the women, young and often graduates, are satisfied with the wages, "so much higher than at home". But they say nothing about the living and working conditions. "If a Moroccan or Romanian worker starts complaining, they won't be hired the following year," says Canamero. So it is up to NGOs and the unions to condemn the overcrowded dormitories, lack of toilets or drinking water in the fields, and the pressure from bosses.

Soltero says that Bionest has "a social policy which ensures people feel good and come back several years running". "Bionest is certainly better than other growers," Viorica Mohan, a Romanian picker, admits, "but they all bend the rules." For instance, contracts are printed in Spanish and include a two-week trial period. Last year some 2,000 Moroccan women were dismissed while still on trial.

A Green member of the European parliament, Hlne Flautre, who visited the area on a parliamentary mission, wants future EU legislation "to set strict standards for employers to improve working conditions for seasonal workers".

This article was first published in Le Monde.
